claims.text: The nanoparticles initially have a near-equiatomic solid-solution structure with a uniform elemental distribution.
Adding 2 wt% Zr during synthesis suppresses atomic diffusion in the nanoparticles.
Suppression of atomic diffusion by Zr prevents phase segregation during high-temperature service.
Preventing phase segregation preserves the near-equiatomic solid-solution structure.
Zr impedes the mobility of the constituent atoms.
Zr increases the kinetic barrier to atomic rearrangement.
Segregation during high-temperature exposure is thermodynamically driven.
Kinetic arrest preserves a uniform, single-phase structure during high-temperature exposure.
After annealing at 1000 K for 4 hours and cooling at 5 K/min, nanoparticles containing 2 wt% Zr will exhibit less phase segregation than undoped controls.
After the specified thermal treatment, nanoparticles containing 2 wt% Zr will retain a more uniform elemental distribution than undoped controls.
The proposed stabilization is applicable to catalytic service over 773–1173 K and thermoelectric service over 473–1923 K.
At sufficiently extreme temperatures or exposure durations, diffusion may eventually permit segregation despite the Zr addition.

contradictions.description: The conditions field broadly presents the hypothesis as applicable across catalytic and thermoelectric ranges extending to 1923 K, whereas the boundary limits applicability to the defined 1000 K treatment and states that it may fail at extreme temperatures. The broader service-range claim is therefore inconsistent with the stated validated boundary.
